title: Give things a name
hook: Store a value once, then use it anywhere in your program.

warmup.q: What does `print("Camera")` show on the screen?
warmup.explain: The quotes only tell Python where the text starts and ends. They are not shown.

warmup.q: A file has three print lines. Which one does Python run first?
warmup.explain: Python reads top to bottom, one line at a time. The order of your lines is the order on screen.

warmup.q: You forget the closing bracket on a print line. What happens?
options: Python shows an error that names the line
warmup.explain: An error is a note, not a failure. It tells you which line to look at.

why.heading: A name for a value
why.text:
A **variable** is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a flight case. Write `crew = "Thabo"` and from then on the name `crew` means Thabo.

The `=` does not mean equals like in maths. It means: store this value under this name.

why.heading: Why bother?
why.text:
Say the call time appears in 20 places in your program, and it moves to 07:30. Without variables you fix 20 lines.

With a variable you write it once:

`call = "07:30"`

Change that one line and every use of it updates. Variables let you say things once.

why.heading: Use it, change it
why.text:
To use a stored value, write the name with no quotes: `print(call)`. With quotes you would just print the word call.

Store something new under the same name and the old value is gone:

`call = "08:00"`

Python runs top to bottom, so lines below see the newest value.

why.heading: Naming rules
why.text:
Use letters, numbers and underscores. No spaces, and never start with a number. `crew_call` is good. `crew call` and `2nd_ad` are not.

Capitals matter: `Call` and `call` are two different names. Pick names that explain themselves, like `day_rate`, not `x`.

why.heading: Names inside text
why.text:
To put a variable inside text, add an `f` before the first quote and wrap the name in curly brackets:

`print(f"Hello {name}")`

Python swaps `{name}` for the stored value. This is an **f-string**. If you use a name you never stored, Python shows a NameError: it does not know that name.

watch.intro: Tap Run. One name, three different values over time.
watch.code:
film = "Imvana"
print(film)
film = "Chasing the Bag"
print(film)
print(f"Now editing {film}")
explain: Line 1 stores the text `Imvana` under the name `film`.
Line 3 stores a new value in the same name. The old one is gone.
The last line uses an f-string: `{film}` is swapped for the current value.
watch.break_it: Break it on purpose: in the last line change `{film}` to `{flim}` and tap Run. The error says `NameError: name 'flim' is not defined`. Python is telling you it never met that name. Fix the spelling and run again.

tasks.title: Print a stored value
tasks.task:
The variable `role` already holds a job. Print it so the screen shows exactly: `Gaffer`

Print the name `role` with no quotes.
tasks.starter:
role = "Gaffer"
# now print the variable role (no quotes)
hints: You want print, then brackets, then the name role inside.
No quotes around role, or you will print the word role.

tasks.title: The call time moved
tasks.task:
The crew call moved to 07:30. Change the stored value so the program shows exactly: `Crew call: 07:30`

Change the variable, not the print line.
hints: Only line 1 needs to change. The print line already uses the variable.
Change the text between the quotes on line 1.

tasks.title: Slate it
tasks.task:
The director wants another take. Change `take` to `"2"` (keep the quotes for now), then print the slate with one f-string so it shows exactly:

`Scene 12, Take 2`
tasks.starter:
scene = "12"
take = "1"
# change take, then print the slate with an f-string
hints: Store a new value in take on its own line, below the old one: take = "2"
Start the print with f before the opening quote. Put {scene} and {take} where the values go.

recap: `name = value` stores a value under a name. The `=` means store.
Use a variable by writing its name with no quotes. Store again to change it.
Names: letters, numbers, underscores, no spaces, not starting with a number.
An f-string `f"Hi {name}"` puts stored values inside text.
NameError means Python does not know that name: check the spelling.

words.meaning: A name that holds a value.
Store a value under a name with `=`.
Text with an f in front that fills in {names}.
Python met a name it was never given.
